{{Short description|Non-informative prior distribution}}
In [[Bayesian statistics]], the '''Jeffreys prior''' is a [[non-informative prior|non-informative]] [[prior distribution]] for a [[parameter space]]. Named after Sir [[Harold Jeffreys]],<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jeffreys H | title = An invariant form for the prior probability in estimation problems | journal = Proceedings of the Royal Society of London |series=Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences | volume = 186 | issue = 1007 | pages = 453–461 | year = 1946 | pmid = 20998741 | doi = 10.1098/rspa.1946.0056 | authorlink = Harold Jeffreys | doi-access =  | jstor = 97883 | bibcode = 1946RSPSA.186..453J }}</ref> its density function is proportional to the [[Square root of a matrix|square root]] of the [[determinant]] of the [[Fisher information]] matrix:

<math display=block>p\left( \theta \right) \propto \left| I (\theta) \right|^{1/2} .\,</math>

It has the key feature that it is invariant under a [[change of coordinates]] for the parameter vector <math display=inline>\theta</math>. That is, the relative probability assigned to a volume of a [[probability space]] using a Jeffreys prior will be the same regardless of the parameterization used to define the Jeffreys prior.  This makes it of special interest for use with [[Scale_parameter|''scale parameters'']].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jaynes ET | title = Prior probabilities. | journal = IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics | date = September 1968 | volume = 4 | issue = 3 | pages = 227–241 | url = http://bayes.wustl.edu/etj/articles/prior.pdf | doi = 10.1109/TSSC.1968.300117 }}</ref> As a concrete example, a [[Bernoulli distribution]] can be parameterized by the probability of occurrence {{mvar|p}}, or by the [[odds]] {{math|1=''r'' = ''p'' / (1 − ''p'')}}. A uniform prior on one of these is not the same as a uniform prior on the other, even accounting for reparameterization in the usual way, but the Jeffreys prior on one reparameterizes to the Jeffreys prior on the other.

In [[maximum likelihood estimation]] of [[exponential family]] models, penalty terms based on the Jeffreys prior were shown to reduce asymptotic bias in point estimates.<ref>{{cite book |first=David |last=Firth |chapter=Bias reduction, the Jeffreys prior and GLIM |title=Advances in GLIM and Statistical Modelling |editor-first=Ludwig |editor-last=Fahrmeir |editor2-first=Brian |editor2-last=Francis |editor3-first=Robert |editor3-last=Gilchrist |editor4-first=Gerhard |editor4-last=Tutz |location=New York |publisher=Springer |year=1992 |pages=91–100 |isbn=0-387-97873-9 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-2952-0_15 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=David |last=Magis |title=A Note on Weighted Likelihood and Jeffreys Modal Estimation of Proficiency Levels in Polytomous Item Response Models |journal=[[Psychometrika]] |volume=80 |issue= |pages=200–204 |year=2015 |doi=10.1007/s11336-013-9378-5 }}</ref>

==Reparameterization==
===One-parameter case===

If <math display=inline>\theta</math> and <math display=inline>\varphi</math> are two possible parameterizations of a [[statistical model]], and <math display="inline">\theta</math> is a [[continuously differentiable]] function of <math display=inline>\varphi</math>, we say that the prior <math display=inline>p_\theta(\theta)</math> is "invariant" under a reparameterization if
<math display=block>p_\varphi(\varphi) = p_\theta(\theta) \left|\frac{d\theta}{d\varphi}\right|,</math>
that is, if the priors <math display=inline>p_\theta(\theta)</math> and <math display=inline>p_\varphi(\varphi)</math> are related by the usual [[change of variables theorem]].

Since the [[Fisher information]] transforms under reparameterization as 
<math display="block">I_\varphi(\varphi) = I_\theta(\theta) \left( \frac{d\theta}{d\varphi} \right)^2,</math>
defining the priors as <math display=inline>p_\varphi(\varphi) \propto \sqrt{I_\varphi(\varphi)}</math> and <math display=inline>p_\theta(\theta) \propto \sqrt{I_\theta(\theta)}</math> gives us the desired "invariance".<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Robert CP, Chopin N, Rousseau J  |title=Harold Jeffreys's Theory of Probability Revisited |journal=Statistical Science |date=2009 |volume=24 |issue=2 |doi=10.1214/09-STS284|doi-access=free |arxiv=0804.3173 }}</ref>

===Multiple-parameter case===

Analogous to the one-parameter case, let <math display=inline>\vec\theta</math> and <math display=inline>\vec\varphi</math> be two possible parameterizations of a statistical model, with <math display=inline>\vec\theta</math> a continuously differentiable function of <math display=inline>\vec\varphi</math>. We call the prior <math display=inline>p_\theta(\vec\theta)</math> "invariant" under reparameterization if
<math display=block>p_\varphi(\vec\varphi) = p_\theta(\vec\theta) ~|\det J|\,,</math>
where <math display=inline>J</math> is the [[Jacobian matrix]] with entries
<math display=block>J_{ij} = \frac {\partial \theta_i}{\partial \varphi_j}.</math>
Since the Fisher information matrix transforms under reparameterization as 
<math display=block>I_\varphi(\vec\varphi) = J^T I_\theta(\vec\theta) J,</math>
we have that
<math display=block>\det I_\varphi(\varphi) = \det I_\theta(\theta) (\det J)^2 </math>
and thus defining the priors as <math display=inline>p_\varphi(\vec\varphi) \propto \sqrt{\det I_\varphi(\vec\varphi)}</math> and <math display=inline>p_\theta(\vec\theta) \propto \sqrt{\det I_\theta(\vec\theta)}</math> gives us the desired "invariance".

==Attributes==
From a practical and mathematical standpoint, a valid reason to use this non-informative prior instead of others, like the ones obtained through a limit in conjugate families of distributions, is that the relative probability of a volume of the probability space is not dependent upon the set of parameter variables that is chosen to describe parameter space.

Sometimes the Jeffreys prior cannot be [[Normalizing constant|normalized]], and is thus an [[improper prior]]. For example, the Jeffreys prior for the distribution mean is uniform over the entire [[Number line|real line]] in the case of a [[Gaussian distribution]] of known variance.

Use of the Jeffreys prior violates the strong version of the [[likelihood principle]], which is accepted by many, but by no means all, statisticians. When using the Jeffreys prior, inferences about <math display=inline>\vec\theta</math> depend not just on the probability of the observed data as a function of <math display=inline>\vec\theta</math>, but also on the universe of all possible experimental outcomes, as determined by the experimental design, because the Fisher information is computed from an expectation over the chosen universe. Accordingly, the Jeffreys prior, and hence the inferences made using it, may be different for two experiments involving the same <math display=inline>\vec\theta</math> parameter even when the likelihood functions for the two experiments are the same—a violation of the strong likelihood principle.

==Minimum description length==

In the [[minimum description length]] approach to statistics the goal is to describe data as compactly as possible where the length of a description is measured in bits of the code used. For a [[parametric family]] of distributions one compares a code with the best code based on one of the distributions in the parameterized family. The main result is that in [[exponential family|exponential families]], asymptotically for large sample size, the code based on the distribution that is a mixture of the elements in the exponential family with the Jeffreys prior is optimal. This result holds if one restricts the parameter set to a compact subset in the interior of the full parameter space{{citation needed|date=September 2018}}. If the full parameter is used a modified version of the result should be used.

==Examples==
The Jeffreys prior for a parameter (or a set of parameters) depends upon the statistical model.

===Gaussian distribution with mean parameter===
For the [[Gaussian distribution]] of the real value <math display=inline>x</math>
<math display=block>f(x\mid\mu) = \frac{e^{-(x - \mu)^2 / 2\sigma^2}}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}}</math>
with <math display=inline>\sigma</math> fixed, the Jeffreys prior for the mean <math display=inline>\mu</math> is
<math display=block>\begin{align} p(\mu) & \propto \sqrt{I(\mu)}
= \sqrt{\operatorname{E}\!\left[ \left( \frac{d}{d\mu} \log f(x\mid\mu) \right)^2\right]}
= \sqrt{\operatorname{E}\!\left[ \left( \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma^2} \right)^2 \right]} \\
& = \sqrt{\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x\mid\mu) \left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\right)^2 dx}
=  \sqrt{\sigma^2/\sigma^4} \propto 1.\end{align}</math>
That is, the Jeffreys prior for <math display=inline>\mu</math> does not depend upon <math display=inline>\mu</math>; it is the unnormalized uniform distribution on the real line — the distribution that is 1 (or some other fixed constant) for all points. This is an [[improper prior]], and is, up to the choice of constant, the unique ''translation''-invariant distribution on the reals (the [[Haar measure]] with respect to addition of reals), corresponding to the mean being a measure of ''location'' and translation-invariance corresponding to no information about location.

===Gaussian distribution with standard deviation parameter===
For the [[Gaussian distribution]] of the real value <math display=inline>x</math>
<math display=block>f(x\mid\sigma) = \frac{e^{-(x - \mu)^2 / 2 \sigma^2}}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}},</math>
with <math display=inline>\mu</math> fixed, the Jeffreys prior for the standard deviation <math display=inline>\sigma > 0</math> is
<math display=block>\begin{align}p(\sigma) & \propto \sqrt{I(\sigma)}
= \sqrt{\operatorname{E}\!\left[ \left( \frac{d}{d\sigma} \log f(x\mid\sigma) \right)^2\right]}
= \sqrt{\operatorname{E}\!\left[ \left( \frac{(x - \mu)^2-\sigma^2}{\sigma^3} \right)^2 \right]} \\
& = \sqrt{\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x\mid\sigma)\left(\frac{(x-\mu)^2-\sigma^2}{\sigma^3}\right)^2 dx}
= \sqrt{\frac{2}{\sigma^2}}
\propto \frac{1}{\sigma}.
\end{align}</math>
Equivalently, the Jeffreys prior for <math display="inline">\log \sigma = \int d\sigma/\sigma</math> is the unnormalized uniform distribution on the real line, and thus this distribution is also known as the '''{{visible anchor|logarithmic prior}}'''. Similarly, the Jeffreys prior for <math display=inline>\log \sigma^2 = 2 \log \sigma</math> is also uniform. It is the unique (up to a multiple) prior (on the positive reals) that is ''scale''-invariant (the [[Haar measure]] with respect to multiplication of positive reals), corresponding to the [[standard deviation]] being a measure of ''scale'' and scale-invariance corresponding to no information about scale. As with the uniform distribution on the reals, it is an [[improper prior]].

===Poisson distribution with rate parameter===
For the [[Poisson distribution]] of the non-negative integer <math display=inline>n</math>,
<math display=block>f(n \mid \lambda) = e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!},</math>
the Jeffreys prior for the rate parameter <math display=inline>\lambda \ge 0</math> is
<math display=block>\begin{align}p(\lambda) &\propto \sqrt{I(\lambda)}
= \sqrt{\operatorname{E}\!\left[ \left( \frac{d}{d\lambda} \log f(n\mid\lambda) \right)^2\right]}
= \sqrt{\operatorname{E}\!\left[ \left( \frac{n-\lambda}{\lambda} \right)^2\right]} \\
& = \sqrt{\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty} f(n\mid\lambda) \left( \frac{n-\lambda}{\lambda} \right)^2}
= \sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}.\end{align}</math>
Equivalently, the Jeffreys prior for <math display="inline">\sqrt\lambda = \int d\lambda/\sqrt\lambda </math> is the unnormalized uniform distribution on the non-negative real line.

===Bernoulli trial===
For a coin that is "heads" with probability <math display=inline>\gamma \in [0,1]</math> and is "tails" with probability <math display=inline>1 - \gamma</math>, for a given <math display=inline>(H,T) \in \{(0,1), (1,0)\}</math> the probability is <math display=inline>\gamma^H (1-\gamma)^T</math>. The Jeffreys prior for the parameter <math display=inline>\gamma</math> is

<math display=block>\begin{align}p(\gamma) & \propto \sqrt{I(\gamma)}
= \sqrt{\operatorname{E}\!\left[ \left( \frac{d}{d\gamma} \log f(x\mid\gamma) \right)^2\right]}
= \sqrt{\operatorname{E}\!\left[ \left( \frac{H}{\gamma} - \frac{T}{1-\gamma}\right)^2 \right]} \\
& = \sqrt{\gamma \left( \frac{1}{\gamma} - \frac{0}{1-\gamma}\right)^2 + (1-\gamma)\left( \frac{0}{\gamma} - \frac{1}{1-\gamma}\right)^2}
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)}}\,.\end{align}</math>

This is the [[arcsine distribution]] and is a [[beta distribution]] with <math display=inline>\alpha = \beta = 1/2</math>. Furthermore, if <math display=inline>\gamma = \sin^2(\theta)</math> then
<math display=block>\Pr[\theta] = \Pr[\gamma] \frac{d\gamma}{d\theta} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{(\sin^2 \theta) (1 - \sin^2 \theta)}} ~2 \sin \theta \cos \theta =2\,.</math>
That is, the Jeffreys prior for <math display=inline>\theta</math> is uniform in the interval <math display=inline>[0, \pi / 2]</math>. Equivalently, <math display=inline>\theta</math> is uniform on the whole circle <math display=inline>[0, 2 \pi]</math>.

===''N''-sided die with biased probabilities===
Similarly, for a throw of an <math display=inline>N</math>-sided die with outcome probabilities <math display=inline>\vec{\gamma} = (\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_N)</math>, each non-negative and satisfying <math display=inline>\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_i = 1</math>, the Jeffreys prior for <math display=inline>\vec{\gamma}</math> is the [[Dirichlet distribution]] with all (alpha) parameters set to one half. This amounts to using a [[Additive_smoothing|pseudocount]] of one half for each possible outcome.

Equivalently, if we write <math display=inline>\gamma_i = \varphi_i^2</math> for each <math display=inline>i</math>, then the Jeffreys prior for <math display=inline>\vec{\varphi}</math> is uniform on the <math display=inline>(N - 1)</math>-dimensional [[unit sphere]] (''i.e.'', it is uniform on the surface of an <math display=inline>N</math>-dimensional [[unit sphere|unit ball]]).

== Generalizations ==
=== Probability-matching prior ===
In 1963, [[Bernard Lewis Welch|Welch]] and [[Harold Williams Peers|Peers]] showed that for a scalar parameter {{mvar|θ}} the Jeffreys prior is "probability-matching" in the sense that [[Posterior predictive distribution|posterior predictive probabilities]] agree with frequentist probabilities and [[credible interval]]s of a chosen width coincide with frequentist [[confidence interval]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |title=On Formulae for Confidence Points Based on Integrals of Weighted Likelihoods |first=B. L. |last=Welch |first2=H. W. |last2=Peers |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society |series=Series B (Methodological) |volume=25 |issue=2 |year=1963 |pages=318–329 |doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1963.tb00512.x }}</ref> In a follow-up, Peers showed that this was not true for the multi-parameter case,<ref>{{cite journal |title=On Confidence Points and Bayesian Probability Points in the Case of Several Parameters |first=H. W. |last=Peers |journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society |series=Series B (Methodological) |volume=27 |issue=1 |year=1965 |pages=9–16 |doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1965.tb00581.x }}</ref> instead leading to the notion of probability-matching priors which are only implicitly defined as the probability distribution solving a certain [[partial differential equation]] involving the [[Fisher information]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Probability matching priors: a review |first=Catia |last=Scricciolo |journal=[[Journal of the Italian Statistical Society]] |volume=8 |at=83 |year=1999 |doi=10.1007/BF03178943 }}</ref>

=== α-parallel prior ===
Using tools from [[information geometry]], the Jeffreys prior can be generalized in pursuit of obtaining priors that encode geometric information of the statistical model, so as to be invariant under a change of the coordinate of parameters.<ref>{{cite journal |first=J. |last=Takeuchi |first2=S. |last2=Amari |title=α-parallel prior and its properties |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=51 |issue=3 |year=2005 |pages=1011–1023 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2004.842703 }}</ref> A special case, the so-called Weyl prior, is defined as a [[volume form]] on a [[Weyl manifold]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=Ruichao |last=Jiang |first2=Javad |last2=Tavakoli |first3=Yiqiang |last3=Zhao |title=Weyl Prior and Bayesian Statistics |year=2020 |journal=Entropy |volume=22 |issue=4 |at=467 |doi=10.3390/e22040467 |doi-access=free |pmc=7516948 }}</ref>
